source_refs.note: Topic 11.5.1, printed pages 253-254. The Interesting Information box on haloalkanes is carried as a sentence.

blocks.text: Substitution reactions of alkanes take place in the presence of light energy through the formation of highly reactive free radicals. An example is the replacement of a hydrogen of an alkane by a halogen atom, halogenation: alkanes react with chlorine and bromine in sunlight or UV light with successive replacement of hydrogen atoms by halogens, the extent of halogenation depending on the amount of halogen used. Reaction with fluorine is highly violent and gives a mixture of carbon, fluorinated alkanes and hydrofluoric acid; iodine does not substitute directly because the reaction is too slow and reversible. The order of reactivity is F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.

items: Initiation: the first step, in which the halogen-halogen bond breaks using energy from UV light: Cl2 with hv gives Cl. + Cl.

Propagation: the second step, in which the radicals formed attack the alkane molecule and generate more free radicals: CH4 + Cl. gives CH3. + HCl, and CH3. + Cl2 gives CH3Cl + Cl. By repetition of this step a mixture of halogen-substituted products (chloroalkanes) is obtained.

Termination: the final step, in which two free radicals react together to form a product. A chlorine radical and an alkyl radical may combine to give a chloroalkane, two chlorine radicals may re-form Cl2, or two alkyl radicals may merge to give an alkane with double the number of carbon atoms; this last mode is rare and gives only traces, but its occurrence is evidence of the free radical mechanism.

blocks.alt: Cl-Cl with two fish-hook arrows from the bond to each Cl, an arrow marked hv, giving Cl. + Cl.
blocks.caption: Initiation step: homolysis of chlorine in UV light (original drawing after the scheme printed on p253 of the textbook).

blocks.alt: Two equations in displayed formulae. CH4 with two fish-hook arrows on one C-H bond + Cl. gives the methyl radical (C with three H and a dot) + H-Cl. The methyl radical + Cl-Cl with two fish-hook arrows on the Cl-Cl bond gives CH3Cl (C with three H and Cl) + Cl.
blocks.caption: Propagation step (original drawing after the scheme printed on p253 of the textbook).

blocks.alt: Three termination equations: i) methyl radical + Cl. gives CH3Cl; ii) methyl radical + methyl radical gives ethane, H3C-CH3, with all bonds shown; iii) Cl. + Cl. gives Cl-Cl.
blocks.caption: Termination step: i) to iii) (original drawing after the scheme printed on p254 of the textbook).

blocks.text: The more chlorine in the mixture to start with, the greater the proportion of chlorine atoms in the chloroalkanes formed: chloromethane CH3Cl, dichloromethane CH2Cl2, trichloromethane CHCl3 (chloroform) and tetrachloromethane CCl4 (carbon tetrachloride) by further substitution with chlorine radicals. Haloalkanes are anaesthetic, their anaesthetic power increasing with the number of halogen atoms, and their use as laboratory solvents is strictly monitored because they are toxic.

blocks.alt: CH3Cl (chloromethane) gives CH2Cl2 (dichloromethane), then CHCl3 (trichloromethane), then CCl4 (tetrachloromethane), with Cl. over each arrow and a red curved arrow over each step labelled Further substitution with Cl. radical.
blocks.caption: Successive substitution of chloromethane to tetrachloromethane (original drawing after the scheme printed on p254 of the textbook).
